talks.title: Keynote Address
talks.teaser: Explains how the EFF's Threat Lab studies surveillance malware and why security workers should push back on stalkerware.
talks.summary:
Eva Galperin, director of cybersecurity at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, opens by explaining what the EFF does and why digital civil liberties now shape everyday life. She describes the organization's mix of tools: impact litigation, a coders' rights program that advises security researchers, international advocacy, grassroots activism, and a technical team that builds privacy tooling such as HTTPS Everywhere and certificate transparency work.

The middle of the talk focuses on the EFF's Threat Lab, a small group that studies surveillance and targeted malware used against journalists, activists and dissidents. She argues that such threats were long ignored because they lacked commercial appeal and were less sophisticated than the nation-state campaigns that security vendors liked to publicize. She points to projects that map police surveillance purchases, research on cell site simulators, and a campaign against government facial recognition.

She closes with stalkerware and domestic abuse, describing the flood of requests she received after offering to help survivors check their devices. Most cases turned out to need account lockdown rather than forensics, which led her to push antivirus vendors to treat stalkerware as unwanted software and to urge companies to make it easier for users to see and revoke access. Her takeaway for attendees is that no formal permission is needed to start research: pick a community, learn where it is underserved, consult a lawyer, and publish.

talks.title: Q&A Keynote
talks.teaser: A live question-and-answer session after a keynote covers facial recognition, stalkerware, internships, and surveillance in Latin America.
talks.summary:
This live question-and-answer session followed a pre-recorded keynote by Eva Galperin of the Electronic Frontier Foundation. The host read questions from the chat and the Discord channel while about eleven minutes remained before the next talk.

On facial recognition, Galperin pointed to a pending United States lawsuit against Clearview AI, where the company argues that scraping social media photos into a biometric database is protected speech. EFF was expected to file an amicus brief in the case. For questions about Canada, she referred listeners to EFF's international team. On parental and family monitoring, she argued that the key line is whether the person being watched is deliberately tricked into not knowing, since that is what makes monitoring stalkerware. She suggested that monitoring a spouse usually points to a deeper problem. An attendee who ran a home lab asked how family monitoring and traffic decryption should be handled, and she treated that as a worthwhile topic. For Latin America, she described a project that tests whether public information request laws work across several governments, and said some governments have used commercially purchased spyware against political opponents. She had not seen this in Venezuela and asked for samples of any government malware found there.

Near the end, the host listed ways to get involved with EFF: summer internships for law students, remote volunteer work with a university student team on its Atlas of Surveillance project, and a technical volunteer mailing list for people with specific skills.

talks.title: Can Artificial Intelligence (AI) Detect Advanced Persistent Threats?
talks.teaser: Examines whether machine learning detectors can spot multi-stage APT intrusions, using a new packet-capture dataset built for testing.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether AI-based products can actually detect advanced persistent threats, the slow and stealthy intrusions carried out by well-funded groups over long periods. The speaker explains why signature-based tools struggle with them and walks through the usual APT stages: reconnaissance, initial foothold, lateral movement, and exfiltration, with log deletion as a final step. Case studies such as the Equifax breach and a Hydra exploit show how these campaigns unfold in practice.

To test detection models, the research team built the DAPT 2020 dataset from packet captures of staged attacks run against a network of deliberately vulnerable virtual machines. Normal user activity was generated alongside the attacks, so attack traffic made up only a small share of the data, and a red team carried out each phase on separate days. The team compared semi-supervised models, including one-class SVM, stacked autoencoders, and an LSTM variant, using precision-recall and ROC metrics. Results varied widely across phases and datasets, and the models performed poorly on lateral movement and exfiltration.

The main takeaway is that reported accuracy figures can hide weak coverage of the attack lifecycle, since many existing datasets omit later stages. The speaker argues that better models are needed, ones that capture time-based context across the phases of an intrusion, and points to the public DAPT 2020 dataset as a starting point for fair evaluation.

talks.title: Can Artificial Intelligence (AI) detect Advanced Persistent Threats?
talks.teaser: Explains how anomaly detection models are applied to network and host logs to spot slow-moving APT activity.
talks.summary:
This Q&A session follows a talk by Ankur Chowdhary on whether artificial intelligence can find Advanced Persistent Threat activity inside a network. The research collected traffic at the boundary between public and private networks, along with Snort alerts, host logs, DNS and web server logs, file server logs and storage system logs. About 84 features were extracted from this traffic and the host data, and the models worked on those features.

On the question of data bias, the speaker noted that APT campaigns can last for weeks or months, so the real signal is small compared with the volume of normal traffic. The team favored anomaly detection models, including one-class SVM, LSTM and stacked autoencoders, and evaluated them with precision rather than ROC curves, since false positive rates can skew results toward the wrong conclusions. Data was gathered over several days in phases: normal baseline traffic first, then reconnaissance, then foothold establishment, which made normal behaviour easier to separate from attack activity.

Questions also covered the risk of manipulation. Attackers can feed falsified data or probe a model to learn which features it uses, a research area known as adversarial attacks that this work did not address. For practitioners, the takeaways are that phased data collection and careful choice of evaluation metrics matter as much as the model itself, and that detection models should be checked for resistance to manipulation.

talks.title: Learning Offensive Security with Project V^3: VulnHub + VirtualBox + Vagrant
talks.teaser: Shows how a project packages VulnHub vulnerable machines as Vagrant boxes so newcomers can start practicing quickly.
talks.summary:
Anthony Radzykewycz and James Green introduce Project V^3, an effort to port machines from VulnHub, a collection of intentionally vulnerable virtual machines, to VirtualBox and publish them as Vagrant boxes on Vagrant Cloud. The aim is to make practice labs easier to set up for newcomers who lack virtualization or sysadmin experience, and to bring in authors of vulnerable machines that are not hosted on VulnHub.

The demo starts with the prerequisites: VirtualBox with its extension pack, Vagrant, and optionally Git. A setup script creates a named internal network, and the attacker VM is attached to it. The presenter clones the project's GitHub repository, finds a beginner machine by searching the directory listing, and runs a single vagrant up command. The box downloads, is imported into VirtualBox, and starts headless. From the attacker host, the presenter confirms the address on the internal network, runs a basic Nmap scan, and opens a web server on port 80 in a browser.

The speakers also cover day-to-day handling. Vagrant halt stops a machine so it can be resumed later from the same directory, while vagrant destroy removes it completely, freeing disk space. Running vagrant up again rebuilds a fresh copy, so learners can reset a lab easily. The takeaway is that the repository reduces lab setup to a few commands, and the speakers invite feedback and contributions from other maintainers of vulnerable machines.

talks.title: Learning Offensive Security with Project V^3: VulnHub + VirtualBox + Vagrant
talks.teaser: Shows how a Vagrant-based project spins up VulnHub vulnerable machines in VirtualBox for offensive security practice.
talks.summary:
The session opens as a Q&A following the talk, where the presenters take questions about Project V^3, a GitHub project that packages machines from VulnHub into Vagrant configurations for VirtualBox. The presenter explains that setup needs VirtualBox with its extension pack, Vagrant, and optionally git, after which a single command brings a lab up. Because the machines are free and the project removes common setup hurdles, it is aimed at newcomers who want to practice.

The discussion then moves to classroom use. By default the attacker and target machines sit on an isolated internal network with no internet or host access, which keeps risky machines contained. For a shared class setup, the presenter suggests moving the target to a bridged network on a central server, which needs extra network work such as VPN access for students. A correction was also made: the removal command must be the vagrant box remove form with the box name, and the README will be updated to reflect it.

The presenters closed by recognizing YoBlog, a machine that was used in a CactusCon 2016 root box competition and that teaches local file inclusion and database exfiltration. They invited exploit developers to contribute machines outside VulnHub. The presenter also described maintenance: of 624 VulnHub machines, 209 had been added so far, and the work proceeds from the newest machines to the oldest.

talks.title: Linux IR: Windows of Opportunity
talks.teaser: Walks through an initial Linux incident response triage of a SystemdMiner sample using open-source logging tools.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that incident response on Linux receives far less attention than Windows, and that the differences come down mostly to tooling, script logging and fleet management. The speaker presents a simplified investigation method built around four questions: who, what, when and where. He suggests choosing log sources with those questions in mind and using the MITRE ATT&CK Linux matrix to decide which log types to collect.

The demonstration detonates a sample from the SystemdMiner malware family on a deliberately vulnerable Jenkins host in a home lab. The lab uses Elastic Security, osquery, Suricata and Zeek. Default alerts flag proxy activity and base64 decoding right away. Process timelines and the analyzer view reveal a chain of shell scripts, a decoded payload that tries to clear the immutable bit on a temporary directory, and a cron entry used for persistence. Network logs show a scan for PostgreSQL on port 5432, downloads through Tor SOCKS proxies, and a check-in from a cryptocurrency miner.

The main takeaways are that Linux lacks an easy equivalent to PowerShell script block logging, so related child processes are hard to tie to one script, and that persistence is almost always present in an intrusion. Process-tree views help, but tooling can hit display limits on large event sets. The speaker argues against running commands such as lsof directly on a suspect host, and suggests remote tools like Velociraptor, Salt or Ansible instead. Building a lab by hand and taking snapshots are recommended for learning and testing.

talks.title: Linux IR: Windows of Opportunity
talks.teaser: Shares practical Linux incident response advice, covering home labs, live-host evidence handling and working with DevOps teams.
talks.summary:
This post-talk Q&A with Jon Wade follows his session on Linux incident response. The discussion opens with why he recommends building a home lab and rebuilding it repeatedly, so responders learn what normal looks like on a Linux system before a real case arrives. He argues that hands-on practice matters more than running a ready-made script that sets the lab up for you.

The middle of the conversation centres on evidence handling. Wade advises against logging into affected hosts to run commands, since that can overwrite memory, expose credentials and compromise a forensically sound disk image. Where possible, he suggests using tools already deployed in the environment, such as configuration management agents or EDR platforms, or writing remote shell scripts that replicate common triage routines. He notes that many enterprise triage tools are simply PowerShell or shell scripts, so teams can build their own. He compares Linux and Windows artifacts, explaining that persistence locations and filesystem metadata differ while the overall IR workflow stays the same. He also recommends early relationships with DevOps teams, with a trained point of contact in each one.

To close, Wade discusses the challenges of aging CentOS and Red Hat-derived distributions, and the scarcity of Linux-only IR roles. He suggests that a responder with Windows experience can learn Linux from the ground up, and that a zero-trust network does not remove the need for incident response. The takeaway is to practise on Linux before an incident happens, keep interaction with live hosts to a minimum, and plan for mixed environments.

talks.title: Hacking with Skynet: How AI is Empowering Adversaries
talks.teaser: Surveys how AI tools help attackers and how machine learning models can be evaded, poisoned or leaked.
talks.summary:
Gavin Klondike opens by framing AI as a double-edged tool: the machine learning that helps defenders with log analysis and anomaly detection can also widen what attackers can do. He separates artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning, then splits the talk into two halves, offensive AI tooling and attacks on machine learning systems.

The first half covers how adversaries could apply AI to social engineering, using generated faces and synthetic voices for fake personas, and to sandbox evasion, where malware checks host features such as process lists and user counts against a threshold. He also covers automated network exploitation frameworks that chain scanners and Metasploit, and the Death Star project that automates a path to domain admin. The second half covers adversarial machine learning: robustness failures, evasion of a naive Bayes spam filter and a commercial antivirus, poisoning of online learners, and data leakage from overfit models. Each attack is paired with possible defenses such as adversarial training, defensive distillation and longer retraining windows.

The closing takeaway is that adversarial examples often fail to transfer between models, so stickers and similar tricks are less practical than headlines suggest, while automation and AI-assisted tradecraft are likely to speed up attackers. Practitioners should treat model inputs, training data and retraining pipelines as attack surface, and watch for automated tooling in intrusions.

talks.title: When Your Memory Forensics Tools Only Tell Half the Story
talks.teaser: Shows how analysts dig past gaps in memory forensics tool output when hunting code injection in Windows processes.
talks.summary:
Memory forensics tools often flag a suspicious process but leave the analyst without the full picture. This talk walks through how to dig further when that happens, using open-source tooling in a REMnux virtual machine. The speaker introduces code injection in general terms, covering DLL injection, reflective DLL injection and process hollowing, and outlines the typical steps malware takes to write code into a running process.

The bulk of the session is three memory-image demonstrations. Two are straightforward: suspicious svchost and explorer processes are pivoted on through process listings, string dumps, YARA scans and malfind output, and an injected executable is confirmed inside a Chrome process. The third case is the harder one. Malfind points at a service host whose memory region shows no visible content, so the analyst checks later pages, finds an embedded PE header, carves the binary out of a dump with a hex editor, and matches it to a known malware family using ClamAV and string analysis.

The takeaway for practitioners is that a flagged memory region with no visible data can still matter, and that knowing how each plugin works helps fill the gaps that automated output leaves behind.

talks.title: Q&A When Your Memory Forensics Tools Only Tell Half the Story
talks.teaser: Covers memory forensics tooling tips, shellcode emulation options, and command-line workflows for finding hidden executable code.
talks.summary:
Ryan hosts this post-talk question-and-answer session with Aaron Sparling after his CactusCon presentation on memory forensics. The conversation opens with audience reaction: viewers were surprised that Volatility includes a built-in shell, and Aaron agrees that it lets an analyst pivot quickly into specific memory regions without leaving the terminal. He describes his usual first step on a sample as isolating a piece of data and generating a strings-based text file that can be searched rapidly.

The middle of the discussion covers the radare2 framework. Aaron explains that he likes staying on the command line to check whether a dumped memory section contains legitimate opcodes, such as a NOP sled followed by shellcode, before deciding whether a full Ghidra project is worth creating. He then turns to shellcode emulation. He notes that scdbg is useful but limited to 32-bit code, and says he has spent recent weeks testing Speakeasy, a FireEye project that emulates shellcode, Windows binaries and drivers. He also mentions a second emulation framework as an alternative.

The closing remarks are brief: Ryan thanks Aaron, and the session moves on to a sponsor giveaway. The practical takeaway is that quick command-line pivots and lightweight emulation can answer early triage questions before heavier reverse engineering tools are needed.

talks.title: Analyzing Suspicious Artifacts (deep dive)
talks.teaser: Walks through static analysis, debugging and emulation of suspicious PE files and shellcode, then links the findings to threat intelligence.
talks.summary:
The talk is a deeper follow-up to an earlier session on triaging suspicious artifacts. The presenters focus on working out what a sample does, what it is for and where it came from, and on how those answers feed threat intelligence and threat hunts. They stress operational security, so all analysis runs offline on an isolated Windows virtual machine rather than in public sandboxes.

The first demo pulls an embedded executable out of a malicious Word document using OLE tooling, then rebuilds the binary from a hex dump in CyberChef. The portable executable is then inspected for imports and header flags, the ASLR setting is disabled, and a debugger check is bypassed in a 32-bit debugger. Watching memory allocations reveals a dumped DLL containing PowerShell strings and a user agent. A stageless Cobalt Strike beacon is identified from its import and export patterns, including a reflective loader. The final section compares two shellcode emulators, shellcode_debug and speakeasy, on a staged beacon, showing the attempted connections to a command-and-control address.

The takeaway is that static inspection, targeted debugging and emulation complement one another. Each step yields indicators and behaviours that can be carried into detections and hunts. The presenters note that this is the first part of a longer series.

talks.title: Q&A Analyzing Suspicious Artifacts (deep dive)
talks.teaser: Live Q&A where the presenters discuss sharing indicators, public sandboxes, and aging out threat intel.
talks.summary:
This live question-and-answer session follows a malware analysis talk, and the two presenters take questions from the chat. Much of the discussion centers on indicator management, including when to share indicators publicly. The presenters suggest that during a fresh incident, waiting until details are published reduces the chance of tipping off an attacker.

The conversation then turns to sandboxing. The presenters briefly explain staged versus stageless payloads, then consider whether private sandboxes could work as public ones. They warn that automatically submitting binaries to public services such as VirusTotal can expose operational security and sensitive data, and that searching a phishing URL in some services can trigger analysis. They also favor crowdsourced detection of fake login pages, and note that trust groups tend to lose value as membership grows.

Toward the end, they consider what happens if a private threat intelligence platform is exposed, and argue that sensitive indicators should carry expiry dates rather than stay private forever. They also raise the scale limits of threat intelligence platforms when teams hoard very large indicator sets. The overall takeaway is that no single right answer exists. Analysts should weigh context before uploading artifacts, and teams should plan retention and sharing policies in advance.

talks.title: The Crimeware Arms Race: Modern Techniques in Malware Armoring & Evasion
talks.teaser: Surveys how malware hides its code and dodges sandboxes, then works through a banking trojan case study.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by separating two goals that malware authors pursue. Armoring is meant to frustrate the analyst studying the code itself, using packers, crypters, obfuscated Windows API calls, junk instructions and payloads that exist only in memory. Evasion is meant to keep malware dormant in analysis environments such as sandboxes and virtual machines, so that it runs only on the machines the author wants to reach.

The speakers then walk through evasion methods seen across the threat landscape. These include checks for virtualization artifacts, CPU core counts, system uptime, recent-document metadata and running analysis tools, along with long sleep periods, user-activity checks and macros that fire only when a document is closed. Network-side tactics are also covered, such as hiding command and control behind Tor back ends, geofencing by location, and tunneling C2 traffic through port-forwarding services. A case study of the Asteroth banking trojan, which targeted Brazilian financial institutions, ties these techniques together. Its late-stage DLL ran a long list of anti-analysis checks, forced a reboot if one failed, and looked up C2 domains hidden in YouTube channel descriptions.

For defenders, the takeaway is that sandboxes need hardening, and that anti-VM tools can reveal which artifacts a virtual machine exposes before it is used for analysis. Because some payloads never touch disk, detection has to look at memory and behavior as well as files, and it should be layered across several controls.

talks.title: The Crimeware Arms Race: Modern Techniques in Malware Armoring and Evasion
talks.teaser: Presenters discuss how malware dodges virtual machines and sandboxes through API hashing and fake user-activity checks.
talks.summary:
This is a short question-and-answer session that follows a malware talk by Nick Biasini and Edmund Brumaghin. The host opens with a giveaway of signed books, then moves into questions about the material covered in the talk.

The discussion starts with API call obfuscation, where malware hides which Windows functions it will call by resolving them through hashing. The speakers point to the Gazdem banking trojan as a memorable case, since analysts had to peel back several decoding stages before the real API targets were visible. The conversation then turns to virtual machine checks. The speakers explain that the answer depends on the threat: banking trojans aim at people's personal machines and so tend to avoid virtual environments, while ransomware typically runs anywhere because encryption is what earns its revenue. Sandbox fingerprinting also comes up, including default hostnames in open-source sandboxes and an enterprise sandbox whose mouse moved during detonation. They also describe malware that waits for the active window to change as proof that a person is at the keyboard.

To close, the host notes that Windows now opens zip archives natively and leaves temporary-folder artifacts behind, and that JScript can run directly from the system. The practical takeaway is that many evasion checks are simple, and that considering a sample's intended victims helps predict which environments it will avoid.

talks.title: Day One Wrapup
talks.teaser: Recaps day one of the virtual conference, covering streaming issues, sponsor thanks, CTF giveaways and the community after-party.
talks.summary:
The host closes out the first day of the ninth CactusCon, which moved from an in-person event to a virtual platform this year. Fourteen talks were chosen from more than 50 submissions, and the day's recordings, Q&A sessions and opening segment are now posted on the video channel. A brief stream outage during a Q&A session lasted only moments, and a cloud-hosted backup streaming server kept the broadcast running after a GPU-equipped streaming box dropped out.

The segment thanks sponsors by tier, including partner, top-tier and supporter sponsors, and notes that sponsors have their own community channels with hiring information. A supporter sponsor offered an Amazon gift card to attendees, and several vendors, including Offensive Security, Hack The Box, No Starch Press and SANS, ran giveaways. The capture-the-flag event has ended, but its challenge boxes and scoreboard stay online overnight without official support. Final results and prizes will be revealed at the closing ceremony the next evening.

Attendees were pointed to the merchandise store and the community Discord, where an after-party chat and audio and visual rooms were scheduled to start that evening. The host mentioned a glitch in the server's join bot that might require leaving and rejoining. The segment ends with a reminder about the next day's closing ceremonies, where the SANS voucher will be given away.

talks.title: Worst of Cybersecurity Reporting
talks.teaser: Two speakers critique 2020 cybersecurity journalism and explain how technologists can help correct misinformation.
talks.summary:
Two speakers, one a tech reporter and one a digital security trainer, revisit poor cybersecurity coverage, this time from 2020, since no CactusCon was held that year. They frame the exercise as a way to improve how stories are written rather than as an attack on individual writers, noting that one bad article does not make an author or publication worthless.

They walk through several examples. A national outlet's headline wrongly tied a former press secretary to Twitter suspension decisions, and the correction left the headline unchanged. Coverage of a phone-forensics vendor's claimed access to Signal blurred the difference between unlocking a device and breaking message encryption, and repeated the claim without supporting data. A paragraph on WeChat relied on a source who did not use the app, while the wider TikTok coverage was mostly solid. A story promoting smartphone voting echoed the vendor's rebuttal of outside researchers' flaw reports and omitted that a bug bounty participant had been referred to authorities. The speakers also discuss when publications should add correction notices.

The takeaways are practical. Check assumptions, verify whether quoted sources are credible and free of conflicts, and read the underlying reports instead of skimming them. Correct errors openly and retract stories whose premise is wrong. Researchers should talk to reporters early, explain which vulnerabilities matter in real-world use, avoid bounty programs that hand researchers to police, and respond quickly to sensational claims.

talks.title: Q&A Worst-of Cybersecurity Reporting
talks.teaser: Two security writers discuss how to keep cybersecurity reporting accurate when stories must move fast.
talks.summary:
This live question-and-answer session follows a talk on poor cybersecurity reporting. The conversation opens with the Verizon breach report and whether its shared taxonomy holds up when organizations map their own threat data onto it. The speakers note that mismatched categories can blur meaning between the source data and the published findings, even though the report is still considered useful.

The discussion then turns to speed versus accuracy. Suggested safeguards include fact-checkers, reading claims back against the original sources, and keeping technical experts on speed dial who can quickly judge whether a story is overblown. The speakers argue that corrections should be treated as normal rather than shameful, and that publications often chase subscribers or time on page rather than raw clicks. Last-minute edits by editors or legal review can distort a technical point and make it sound vague.

For organizations, the advice is to avoid generic security buzzwords and instead publish specifics such as design details, white papers, and candid statements of what a product cannot do. Readers vetting a journalist are encouraged to look at past work and ethics rather than technical credentials, and PR teams should be pushed to connect reporters with the right engineers. The session closes with a brief look at reporting on stolen documents, where the bar is public interest and the decision is best made with editors.

talks.title: Personal Branding, Safely: Protect yourself from a world of creeps and criminals
talks.teaser: Explains how doxing works and walks through a personal risk assessment and steps to protect your online identity.
talks.summary:
Personal branding brings networking, career opportunities and visibility, but it also makes people easier to target for harassment, stalking and doxing. The talk argues that anyone with data online faces some risk, and that the realistic goal is to reduce exposure and prepare responses rather than reach perfect privacy. It traces the term doxing back to 1990s hacker culture and surveys cases involving celebrities, activists, journalists and political figures, including people who revealed too much about themselves.

Much of the information attackers use is gathered legally from social media, people-search sites, breach data, archived web pages and photo metadata. A live demonstration starts from a single website and pivots through reverse image search, professional profiles and a people-search lookup to map an individual's online footprint. Recommended defenses include catch-all email addresses, unique usernames, device-based multi-factor authentication, segregated IoT networks, credit freezes, a separate phone number and mailing address, pruning old posts, opting out of data brokers, and limiting geotags and location access.

Monitoring covers login alerts, bank notifications, search alerts for your name, credit monitoring and tax-fraud indicators. If harassment starts, the speaker advises staying calm, capturing screenshots, reporting to platforms, ending active sessions and leaning on a support network. Resources mentioned include Maltego Community Edition and a guide to removing data from people-search sites.

talks.title: Q&A Keynote
talks.teaser: Follows a pre-recorded keynote with a live Q&A on security questions, old online accounts and lasting personal data.
talks.summary:
This live segment followed a pre-recorded keynote by April C. Wright. The host opened by thanking her and running a prize giveaway, then read through audience comments. Viewers responded most to her explanation of where the term doxing came from and to her point that security questions are weak when the answers are facts anyone can look up. Several attendees described their own workarounds, such as inventing answers to security prompts or using unrelated phrases in place of real details. Another commenter mentioned that a professional networking profile can be hidden from search engine results, which they had not known about.

A viewer asked what to do about email accounts and sign-ups made as a teenager and forgotten since. Wright explained that the answer depends on whether the original email address is still accessible. If it is not, the practical route is to contact the service provider directly, supply details about the account and possibly proof of identity, and ask for access to be restored. She stressed that anything posted online tends to persist, and that a service which does not verify identity may keep sending mail to an address the person can no longer control.

The session closed with thanks from the host and a pointer to the next talk on the schedule. The practical takeaways are to treat security question answers as passwords, to avoid answers that can be found in public records or social media, and to review old accounts when access to their recovery email is still available.

talks.title: Stealing a Password Through Interpretive Dance, and Other Wild Video Game Hacks
talks.teaser: Walks through six exploits in Super Smash Bros. Melee netplay and open-source Magic: The Gathering software.
talks.summary:
The talk covers six security issues the speaker found while tinkering with video games and open-source projects rather than during a dedicated bug hunt. The first set targets Super Smash Bros. Melee online play, which uses a rollback netcode that sends controller inputs peer to peer over UDP. A packet that claims a frame far beyond its real contents triggers an out-of-bounds read: a crash at large values, and leaked heap memory at smaller ones, possibly including a player's account key. Because streams and replay files reveal the resulting in-game actions, the speaker shows how an attacker could recover that data.

Further issues concern the ENet networking library and Magic: The Gathering software. ENet's fixed peer table can be exhausted by spoofed connection attempts, a denial of service akin to a SYN flood, and its predictable sequence numbers and peer IDs make it feasible to forge a disconnect packet and end a live match. In Cockatrice, the deck shuffle uses a Mersenne Twister, whose output can be reversed to recover the seed and predict deck order. XMage's remoting layer deserializes untrusted Java objects, allowing a resource-exhaustion attack and arbitrary command execution through a gadget chain.

The overarching lesson is that game networking and open-source game tools often lack protections that web services take for granted, such as randomized sequence numbers, safe deserialization and cryptographic randomness. Anyone running a custom protocol exposed to untrusted peers should assume hostile input and validate lengths and identifiers. Some of these issues were fixed, while others were left open by their maintainers.

talks.title: Stealing a password through interpretive dance, and other wild video game hacks
talks.teaser: Follows up on a Super Smash Bros. Melee replay-file exploit, covering the bug, its patch history, and the cheating risks it raises.
talks.summary:
This Q&A follows a prerecorded talk by Dan Petro on video game hacking, centred on a flaw in the replay files of Super Smash Bros. Melee. The session opens with stream giveaways, then moves to the talk itself, which the speaker recorded over several days and presented as a produced video rather than slides.

Discussion turns to the exploit. The first bug, a read overflow in the replay parser, was hard to fix: an earlier patch attempt in October broke replay handling, and the fix only shipped recently. The speaker says the exploit has not been made public. He explains that no good library exists for editing the replay format, which he plans to build, and that such a tool could enable match fabrication, since replays serve as proof of results at tournaments.

The conversation then compares fighting game play with chess servers, covering latency sensitivity and why web-based games behave differently. For practitioners, the main takeaway is to treat files that act as proof of activity as untrusted input, and to weigh how both a patch and any editing tool could be misused before release.

talks.title: Introduction to Car Hacking Basics
talks.teaser: Shows how to set up a virtual CAN bus lab and inject packets into a simulated car without owning a vehicle.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a disclaimer and the motivation for practicing car hacking in a virtual setting, since experimenting on a real vehicle is costly and can cause damage. The speaker explains that modern cars contain many interconnected computers linked by the Controller Area Network, or CAN bus, a design dating back to the early 1990s that has changed little since. The OBD-II port offers a standardized connection to that bus, with fixed pin assignments for CAN high and CAN low.

The demonstration runs on an Ubuntu virtual machine where the speaker builds can-utils and ICSim, a simulated instrument cluster with controls, and attaches it to a virtual CAN interface. Traffic is observed in Wireshark and with a sniffer tool that highlights changing identifiers. Frames are then sent by hand and in a simple loop to drive the simulated speedometer, and a seeded randomizer shows how the identifier mapping can be changed so that earlier findings no longer apply.

The closing section covers hardware for real vehicles, comparing an inexpensive USB-to-CAN adapter, an Arduino with a CAN shield, and a dedicated CANtact interface, each with different buffer and capability trade-offs. The main takeaway is that the process is tedious and relies on patience: recording traffic, correlating it with injected messages, and testing repeatedly. Working through a virtual lab first lets a beginner learn the workflow without risking a car.

talks.title: Q&A Introduction to Car Hacking Basics
talks.teaser: Answers beginner questions on car hacking, from entry-level tools like the CANtact to finding local meetups.
talks.summary:
Host Ryan opens a live Q&A with K "Turb0Yoda" Singh, a car hacking enthusiast. Ryan recalls his own early tinkering with performance data loggers and his attempt to crack their licensing software, which leads into a conversation about how vehicle tinkering can grow into security work.

Singh describes his entry point as plain curiosity: he connected a laptop to his car to see what would happen, and he especially enjoys emulating the virtual instrument cluster. The discussion touches on the CAN bus and OBD-II, which is mandatory on modern vehicles, and on how easily a diagnostic port can be reached. For hardware, he uses an ELM327 for basic engine codes and prefers the CANtact for broader work. He notes that the CANtact is open-source hardware with its board files published online, and that an Arduino with a CAN shield offers a cheaper route.

Viewer questions covered a car kit Singh had not used and similar products he could not name. For getting involved, he pointed to Open Garages, a directory of local meetups where people work on cars together, and encouraged anyone wanting to start a group to do so. He warned newcomers to budget for a spare car in case they break their own. Links to repositories and tools were promised for the Q&A channel.

talks.title: The Full Purple Juice, Not the Watered-Down Stuff
talks.teaser: Walks through a six-week purple team exercise that measures detection coverage of adversary behaviors using existing tools.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a six-week purple team engagement run for a real client, the National Motor Freight Traffic Association. The speakers took on cyber threat intelligence, red team and blue team roles, working inside the production environment under a strict rule of no new technology spending, so only existing controls could be tuned.

The first week set a baseline with a simple campaign that went almost entirely unseen. Each later week emulated a different threat group of rising sophistication, drawn from public adversary emulation plans. For each one the team enabled more Sysmon event types, forwarded logs to the existing SIEM, and built correlation logic so that chains of behavior triggered alerts. Testing also exposed gaps such as outbound RDP and standard users in an enterprise admin group, and a team that believed PowerShell was unused produced hundreds of alerts once it was monitored.

Detection rose from about 6 percent of tested behaviors at baseline to roughly 64 percent by the end. The speakers stressed that full coverage is unrealistic and that each organization should find its own natural detection rate. Practical takeaways include testing in production so controls reflect real conditions, involving people and process alongside technical checks, and measuring response times once alerts exist.

talks.title: The full purple juice, not the watered down stuff
talks.teaser: Two practitioners discuss how collaboration between offensive and defensive teams makes purple teaming more effective.
talks.summary:
This live question-and-answer session follows a earlier talk on purple teaming. The host opens with several giveaways, including a digital forensics book and four months of a cyber range subscription, and mentions a free SANS course to be awarded at the closing ceremonies. Audience questions follow about the speakers' custom hoodie designs, which are sold through a swag store whose proceeds go to rhino conservation.

The main discussion covers how the speakers came to purple teaming. One ran an offensive team of roughly 145 ethical hackers at a large bank. He found that isolated, zero-knowledge red team engagements delivered limited value, so his team began working directly with defenders to address problems in people, process and technology. The other speaker describes moving away from ego-driven red teaming and giving talks on a collaborative approach, which he later found already had a name.

The takeaway for practitioners is that offense and defense working on the same goals tends to produce faster, more practical fixes than adversarial testing alone. The session closes with a reminder of a hands-on purple team workshop scheduled later the same day.

talks.title: Extracting a Bootloader's AES Key via a Power Analysis Side Channel Attack
talks.teaser: Shows how a power analysis side channel attack can recover an AES bootloader key from a Microchip microcontroller.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why third-party accessory makers struggle with GoPro's Hero5 protections, and why encrypted firmware updates made key extraction hard through software alone. The target was a Microchip SAMD21 microcontroller with a small attack surface, so common routes such as debug interfaces, fuzzing and known vulnerabilities did not get far. Timing attacks, voltage glitching and electromagnetic fault injection were set aside in favour of power analysis.

The middle section covers the cryptographic background: the AES decryption rounds, the key schedule, and why the inverse shift step can be ignored for this purpose. Hamming weight models link power draw to the data moving across the chip's buses, and correlation power analysis matches guessed key bytes against measured traces. The setup used a ChipWhisperer, a shunt resistor with a differential probe, and an oscilloscope that oversampled the target's internal clock. Traces were aligned with a sum of absolute differences filter, and the round-ten key was recovered from about 150 traces in the demonstrated run, with any stubborn bytes brute forced.

The closing advice is to build a mockup of the target first, learn the tooling on it, and watch for rabbit holes, since simpler routes or faster methods such as electromagnetic fault injection may exist.

talks.title: Extracting a Bootloader's AES Key via a Power Analysis Side Channel Attack
talks.teaser: Follows up on a power analysis side channel attack with answers on chip hardening, learning hardware analysis, and tools.
talks.summary:
This segment is a live Q&A with Mark Kirschenbaum after his talk on extracting a bootloader's AES key with a power analysis side channel attack. The host opens by asking what motivated the talk and how he got into hardware work. He explains that he was inspired by an earlier security camera talk at the conference, and that about two decades of building programmers and debuggers gave him a practical route into analyzing devices.

The discussion then turns to defenses. Asked whether manufacturers could make this kind of attack impossible, he says destroying the chip is not the answer. Dedicated security chips use hardening such as differential signaling to make leakage harder to measure, while general-purpose microcontrollers tend to be much noisier and easier to observe. He says some leakage remains in almost every design, so hardening reduces the risk rather than removing it.

For newcomers, he points to low-cost boards and open tools for JTAG and side-channel learning, and to a community of hardware hackers who share their tooling online. He closes by mentioning that a hardware hacking village may return to the conference once in-person events resume, giving attendees a chance to try these techniques hands-on.

talks.title: Hands-on Purple Team Workshop
talks.teaser: Guides attendees through a hands-on purple team exercise that pairs adversary emulation with blue team detection.
talks.summary:
The workshop opens by explaining purple teaming as a working arrangement between threat intelligence, red team and blue team staff rather than a separate job title. The presenter traces how organizations moved from vulnerability scanning to penetration testing and then to adversary-focused exercises, and shows how a plan built from intelligence on groups that target hospitals gives the exercise its direction.

Attendees then work in an isolated lab with a domain controller, a Windows member server, a Linux host and an attack platform. They build a command and control campaign in SCYTHE, emulate behaviors mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, and switch to the defender role to look for indicators of compromise using Sysmon and Wireshark. Along the way the talk covers exercise roles, preparation steps such as opening a case and confirming that security tools run on target systems, and how to record results during the exercise.

The session closes with lessons learned. Participants are encouraged to document both detected and missed behaviors, make quick tuning changes, and repeat techniques that went unseen. The main takeaway is that a purple team exercise can raise detection coverage through better process and collaboration, without necessarily buying new technology. The lab virtual machines from the event are no longer available.

talks.title: Reverse Engineering Websites
talks.teaser: Shows how to infer a website's architecture and logic from its responses to support later security testing.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a common limit in web testing: without source code, accounts or server access, a tester has to work out how an application is built from the outside. The speaker presents reverse engineering of websites as a way to build an accurate mental model, drawing on recognition-based decision making and on combining inductive and deductive reasoning to form and check assumptions. Common architectural patterns, such as presentation, logic and data tiers, give a starting point for reading unfamiliar systems.

A worked example uses a large public wiki whose code is open, so each guess can be checked against the real software. Response headers and cookies reveal a caching layer, the caching technology, and region-based content. Two URL structures serving the same page point to a front controller, while a REST-style endpoint, a separate logging beacon and a page-controller pattern suggest additional code bases and servers. The speaker notes that fingerprinting tools can speed up identification but do not show how the pieces fit together.

For practitioners, the main lesson is to map functions and parameters through recognised patterns, then use that map to target likely weak points. Alternative input routes, URL rewriting and cache behaviour can open angles such as server-side request forgery through document export, cache-related attacks and second-order issues in logging. Timing differences can also reveal hidden behaviour that is otherwise invisible.

talks.title: Q&A Reverse Engineering Websites
talks.teaser: A short interview traces how a pen tester moved from automating routine checks to deeper manual app analysis.
talks.summary:
This short Q&A segment from CactusCon opens with the host handing out several prizes, including hardware badges and signed books, before turning to the guest's background. The conversation centers on how the guest approached reverse engineering websites over the course of a long penetration testing career.

The guest recounts starting penetration testing around 2010, when a heavy workload of roughly fifty engagements a year pushed him to learn the common vulnerability classes well and then automate the repeatable parts of testing. He describes how the repetition eventually became tedious, which led him to spend more time on the parts automation could not reach, such as reasoning about how an application was built and what its developers were likely to have done. After moving to a firm with fewer, longer engagements, he had room to dig deeper and refined his process within about a year.

The segment closes with the guest noting that it has taken him a while to put this method into words and teach it, because his long experience makes it hard to judge what others already know. For a practitioner, the main takeaway is the progression from broad knowledge and automation toward manual, reasoning-driven analysis of how a web application behaves.

talks.title: MQTT: Tiny Protocol, Big Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Explains how exposed MQTT brokers are found on the internet and how their weak defaults can be enumerated.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces MQTT, a lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed for unreliable links such as oil rigs and small sensors. It walks through the roles of publishers, brokers, subscribers and topics, and gives a simple home automation example. Common uses are shown in connected cars, smart homes and industrial plants. The speaker explains that the protocol was built for trusted parties, so security was not a core goal.

The middle section reviews the main weak points: denial of service through broker overload and client ID spoofing, weak or missing authentication, shared device certificates, loose topic authorization with wildcards, unpatched software, and unencrypted transport on the standard port. The speaker then scans the internet with Masscan, a fast nmap-style scanner, after a subnetting mistake widened a run to about 16 million hosts. Roughly 1,000 hosts answered on the unencrypted port. A script filtered for brokers that accepted anonymous connections, and the mqtt-pwn toolkit was used to browse topics on a few of them. The talk stresses that scanning is only legal and ethical when authorized.

The closing argument is that cloud migration brings default TLS, identity integration and anomaly detection, but also widens exposure and often drops redundancy practices. The takeaways are that MQTT is widespread, often misconfigured, lacks native encryption and authentication, and makes per-device credentials hard to manage. Compromising one device to steal a certificate is therefore a common foothold.

talks.title: MQTT: Tiny Protocol, Big Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Closes with a live Q&A on MQTT botnets, weak IoT configurations, and why network segmentation matters.
talks.summary:
In this closing Q&A session of CactusCon, host Ryan talks with Tracie Martin about her talk on MQTT, the lightweight messaging protocol used by many IoT devices. She explains that her interest grew out of her IoT security work, where she applied an attacker's mindset to find the most efficient targets. Because MQTT routes traffic through a central broker, a single compromise there can affect many devices at once.

The discussion turns to real-world abuse. Martin notes that MQTT-based botnets so far have mostly aimed at denial of service by overwhelming brokers, and that poorly configured brokers combined with poorly configured devices create serious risk. She describes her path into IoT from earlier industrial IoT work and traditional application security roles, and says she began presenting after realizing that practical, everyday knowledge is valuable to the community.

On whether manufacturers can be pushed to recommend network segmentation, she points to existing regulatory guidance but says low-cost devices rarely ship with security features because buyers will not pay extra. She argues that cloud and connectivity providers should make secure defaults easier to adopt. She illustrates the problem with a home camera that allowed only six-digit passwords and kept remote access always on, and with shared certificates copied across many devices, which let one device impersonate another. The session ends with conference giveaways and pointers to other events.

talks.title: Closing Ceremonies
talks.teaser: Wraps up the virtual CactusCon 9 with staff thanks, attendance figures, finances, and giveaways.
talks.summary:
The closing ceremony for the ninth CactusCon ends a conference that moved entirely online this year. The host opens by describing how the virtual event came together, including several hiccups: a stream dropout during a Q&A, a registration bot that failed before the first day, and a GPU failure on the streaming machine. Staff, volunteers, artists, keynote speakers, workshop instructors and sponsors are thanked in turn, and the pre-recorded talks released in premiere mode with live Q&A are recapped.

The middle of the segment reviews the numbers. General admission registrations passed 3,000, and the Discord server logged thousands of messages and dozens of help tickets. A capture-the-flag event drew several hundred players and more than 13,000 flag submissions, and a separate kids CTF was announced. The finance section explains that the nonprofit ended the year out of the red, mainly because virtual delivery avoided venue, art, badge and merchandise costs, and that sponsor and community donations are being reinvested.

The close covers sponsor giveaways, an open online store, a community Discord that will host the after party, and plans to keep an online presence for future events. The main takeaway for organizers is that a virtual conference can work with a volunteer crew, free tooling and careful planning, though it still needs contingency plans for technical failures.

talks.title: Hacking Back Scammers
talks.teaser: Explains how student researchers run scam-baiting calls, from building an isolated setup and persona to collecting intelligence.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the scale of phone, romance, tech support and employment scams, citing 2021 loss figures and noting that older and younger people tend to be targeted by different scam types. The speakers, students from Arizona State University, present their capstone project as a way to gather actionable intelligence on scammers so victims can be warned and cases reported. They stress that the work is meant to stay within the law.

The core of the talk is a scam-baiting checklist. The team builds an isolated environment with virtual machines, a VPN, a VoIP phone service and separate email accounts, and configures a Windows machine to resemble an ordinary victim's computer. Before each call they set a goal, which is mainly to waste the scammer's time, then pick a scam and research it using community forums and scam-number databases. They build a fake persona whose details can pass basic checks, including addresses, area codes, and card numbers that pass a Luhn check. During calls, roles are split between the person on the phone, a note-taker, a researcher and someone who keeps the persona consistent, with shared notes kept live.

A case study showed a caller keeping a scammer engaged for well over an hour, until the scammer was sent a fake verification link that led to a dating site and exposed network details. Reports go to different places depending on the scam: domain abuse teams, platforms such as Instagram, or the FBI's cybercrime unit. The main takeaways are to define a clear goal, keep the persona believable and consistent, isolate the environment carefully, and expect scammers to grow more suspicious over time.
